external_integration_coverage: Zig shipped a first-party package manager only in version 0.11 (August 2023), using build.zig.zon manifests that 'fetches dependencies directly from URLs, usually tarballs on GitHub' rather than a central registry.
Zig 'does not have an official package repository like npm or crates.io,' relying instead on informal community registries such as Zigistry.

Community-maintained integrations exist for common external systems: native PostgreSQL drivers (pg.zig, multiple forks), and a Zigistry-listed collection covering 'Postgres and SQLite, S3, an HTTP client, a job queue in your database, JWT, cache, config, password hashing,' plus Redis client SDKs and HTTP/1.1/2/3-over-QUIC/WebSocket/TLS 1.3/protobuf network frameworks.

There is no official first-party AWS/GCP/Azure SDK; the community 'aws-sdk-for-zig' project explicitly 'mimics the aws c libraries for its work' and still has gaps (e.g. 'WebIdentityToken is not yet implemented').

Community forum threads show integration gaps being actively worked around rather than solved by mature libraries, e.g. users asking for a native EdgeDB driver or MySQL driver options for Zig web projects.

A 2026 supply-chain analysis states Zig's package identifiers are not yet integrated with cross-ecosystem tooling: 'Zig doesn't have a PURL type yet, so Zig packages can't be referenced in SBOMs, advisory databases, or cross-ecosystem tooling in a standardized way,' and that adoption of tools like Dependabot, Renovate, and Snyk is still pending: 'they're still waiting on Dependabot, Renovate, and Snyk to care.'
The same analysis notes Zig also lacks trusted-publishing / provenance infrastructure comparable to PyPI or npm: 'If Zig gets a central registry, it needs this infrastructure too.'

A mid-2026 follow-up piece confirms there is still no central Zig package registry, and that package availability, account recovery, and abuse handling 'all fall to whichever source host the URL points at, which in practice is overwhelmingly GitHub' rather than a first-party integration layer.

Third-party tooling to embed Zig into other ecosystems does exist (e.g. the Vezel Zig SDK integrates Zig/C/C++ builds into the .NET/MSBuild/NuGet pipeline), showing some cross-ecosystem integration capability built on Zig's C-toolchain and cross-compilation features, but this is a community project, not an official Zig Software Foundation deliverable.
implemented_platform_coverage: Zig documents an explicit four-tier target support system: 'Zig's level of support for various targets is broadly categorized into four tiers with Tier 1 being the highest.' (ziglang.org platform-support page).

Zig 0.14.0 release notes describe a major expansion of correctly cross-compilable and runnable targets: 'the list of targets that Zig can correctly cross-compile to and run on has been greatly expanded,' explicitly fixing toolchain problems for arm/thumb, mips/mips64, powerpc/powerpc64, riscv32/riscv64, and s390x.

Zig 0.16.0 release notes show continued CI-verified target expansion: 'aarch64-freebsd, aarch64-netbsd, loongarch64-linux, powerpc64le-linux, s390x-linux, x86_64-freebsd, x86_64-netbsd, and x86_64-openbsd are now tested natively in Zig's CI.'
Zig supports WebAssembly natively; historic release notes note wasm32 became guaranteed-available via LLVM and that 'this makes WebAssembly work out-of-the-box in Zig.'

Cross-compilation to many OS/arch/libc combinations (including musl variants) is demonstrated end-to-end, e.g. 'zig cc -target x86_64-linux-gnu' and 'zig cc -target loongarch64-linux-musl' producing runnable binaries verified under QEMU/Wine.

Wikipedia's infobox on Zig lists supported OS as 'Cross-platform: Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, Windows' and platforms as 'x86-64, ARM64, WebAssembly' with Tier 2 covering 'ARM, IA-32, RISC-V, MIPS64, POWERPC64, SPARC64.'

Zig has no official, upstream-merged Android or iOS cross-compilation support: an unofficial fork states 'Zig itself doesn't cross-compile to Android or iOS out of the box — no bundled libc data for Bionic, no bundled iOS SDK headers,' and that the corresponding pull requests submitted upstream 'were removed from the upstream repository without public explanation.'

The same fork confirms Android support (API 21-37, multiple ABIs) is 'working, used in production for cross-compiling a game engine to Android' only via this third-party, non-affiliated fork, not via official Zig releases.

Zig's own overview page frames the tier system as the mechanism for communicating target support levels and notes that even Tier 1 targets 'may have a few disabled tests as we work towards 100% test pass rate,' i.e. even the top tier is not yet fully mature pre-1.0.

evidence.notes: Single-language shard: only the 'Zig' key is returned for each metric per the language-sharded packet-only convention; the runner merges disjoint per-language shards. Scores reflect Zig's officially-implemented (not merely theoretically portable) platform breadth and the current maturity of its external-system integration/supply-chain tooling as of the snapshot date, using the frozen rubrics above applied identically across all 10 benchmarked languages.

bands_0_100.0-19: essentially no integrations beyond raw C FFI
bands_0_100.40-59: decent breadth of community-maintained integrations across common categories (DB drivers, HTTP/TLS, some cloud via unofficial SDKs) but no official first-party vendor SDKs, no central package registry, and no SBOM/dependency-scanner integration
bands_0_100.60-79: broad third-party integration coverage across most major categories, some official vendor support, partial supply-chain tooling support
bands_0_100.80-100: official first-party integrations plus thriving third-party ecosystem across virtually all major external systems, with full SBOM/dependency-scanner/registry support

metric.external_integration_coverage.definition: Breadth and reliability of working integrations with external systems (databases, cloud provider services, messaging/network protocols, web frameworks), plus the maturity of supply-chain/registry tooling (SBOM, dependency scanners, centralized package registry) that lets those integrations be tracked and consumed reliably.

bands_0_100.30-49: a couple of desktop OSes only, no WASM/embedded/mobile
bands_0_100.50-69: broad desktop OS + wide architecture coverage + WASM + freestanding/embedded, but no official mobile support (mobile only via unmerged third-party forks)
bands_0_100.70-89: desktop+WASM+embedded plus partial/experimental first-party mobile support
bands_0_100.90-100: first-party, CI-verified support across desktop, mobile, embedded and WASM

metric.implemented_platform_coverage.definition: Breadth and quality of actually-implemented (not merely theoretically portable) target platforms: hosted OS families, CPU architecture breadth, freestanding/embedded (bare-metal) support, WebAssembly support, and official first-party mobile (Android/iOS) support, weighted by how rigorously each is verified (CI-tested tiers vs. experimental/unofficial).
